alternatives: Levetiracetam and valproate are both effective in generalized epilepsies; valproate is appropriate in a man with normal liver function.
Lacosamide and other sodium-channel agents share the aggravation concern of phenytoin in generalized epilepsies and are not preferred here.
interactions: Phenytoin, fosphenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin, pregabalin and vigabatrin in idiopathic generalized epilepsy: these agents can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures and are avoided in this syndrome, although phenytoin does terminate generalized tonic-clonic status if no alternative is available.
Levetiracetam + no other medication: no pharmacokinetic interaction; it is renally cleared, and the dose is reduced for a creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min (creatinine here 0.9 mg/dL).
Valproate + lorazepam: valproate inhibits glucuronidation and raises lorazepam exposure, adding sedation.
Lorazepam, repeated doses: additive respiratory depression; monitor the airway and be ready to intubate.
output.proposed: Levetiracetam, valproate, lacosamide or phenytoin after lorazepam in a man with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy

output.query: Status epilepticus treatment and antiseizure medication choice in idiopathic generalized epilepsy

results.finding: Convulsive status epilepticus is treated at 5 minutes with an adequately dosed benzodiazepine; IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg to a maximum of 4 mg per dose may be repeated once after 5 to 10 minutes.
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective as second-line agents for benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive status epilepticus.

Seizures continuing after a benzodiazepine and an adequately dosed second-line agent are refractory and are treated with an anaesthetic infusion under continuous EEG; continuous EEG is recommended when consciousness does not return.
Convulsive status epilepticus is defined at 5 minutes of continuous convulsive activity, with long-term consequences expected beyond 30 minutes.

output.summary: Convulsive status epilepticus is treated at 5 minutes with an adequately dosed benzodiazepine, repeated once if needed [Glauser_2016; ILAE_2015_SE], and levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective second-line agents in ESETT [ESETT_2019]. Seizures persisting after both tiers are refractory and are treated with an anaesthetic infusion under continuous EEG [Brophy_2012]. In idiopathic generalized epilepsies, sodium-channel blocking agents such as carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin and vigabatrin, can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures, which is why they are avoided for maintenance in this syndrome.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Levetiracetam undetectable (below 2.0 mcg/mL), confirming the lapse; venous lactate 8.2 mmol/L with bicarbonate 18, CK 1840 U/L, troponin I 0.06 ng/mL and WBC 14.8 x10^9/L after prolonged convulsions; electrolytes, calcium, magnesium and renal function normal
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function, levetiracetam level, CK
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; the levetiracetam level because he is on an antiseizure medication. The cause is evident from the history, so a toxicology screen is reasonable but not required [Brophy_2012]. CK because rhabdomyolysis follows prolonged convulsions and decides the fluid management.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No hemorrhage, mass, midline shift or hydrocephalus
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast head CT after stabilization
action_criteria.rationale: Status epilepticus in a patient with known epilepsy still needs structural exclusion when it is his first episode of status and he has not returned to baseline [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Initial generalized suppression then a recovering, reactive slow background with interictal generalized 3-4 Hz polyspike-wave bursts and no electrographic seizures: the convulsive status has stopped and no non-convulsive status follows
action_criteria.label: Continuous video-EEG to exclude ongoing non-convulsive seizures after the convulsions stop
action_criteria.rationale: Up to one in seven patients remains in non-convulsive status after the motor activity stops, so a patient who is not back to baseline needs EEG rather than observation alone [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal MRI: no hippocampal sclerosis, cortical malformation, mass, hemorrhage or restricted diffusion
action_criteria.label: MRI brain on an epilepsy protocol if any doubt remains about the syndrome
action_criteria.rationale: The syndrome was established by video-EEG 8 years ago and the precipitant is identified, so MRI is low yield; it is reasonable only because this is his first episode of status epilepticus [Glauser_2016].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: The check names the agents that worsen myoclonus in this syndrome, so they are excluded from maintenance; it confirms that his own drug has no interaction and is dosed by renal function, and that one alternative increases benzodiazepine exposure
action_criteria.label: Drug-interaction check of the candidate second-line ASMs in a generalized epilepsy
action_criteria.rationale: He takes no other medication, so no interaction forbids a drug; the check is recommended because the syndrome itself restricts the maintenance choice (agents that aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures) [Glauser_2016].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General cited evidence on benzodiazepine dosing, the equivalence of the three second-line agents, and the aggravating agents in generalized epilepsy
action_criteria.label: Literature on second-line treatment of convulsive status epilepticus
action_criteria.rationale: Optional background on the treatment tiers and on ASM choice in generalized epilepsies; it is not a clinical step [ESETT_2019].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not use carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin, pregabalin or vigabatrin for maintenance in this syndrome: they aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures.
Do not start empiric antimicrobials or draw blood cultures for the temperature of 38.1 C in the absence of any source.
Do not treat the troponin of 0.06 ng/mL as an acute coronary syndrome with antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy in a 36-year-old after prolonged convulsions.
Do not discharge him without a dispensed supply of levetiracetam, a refill plan and epilepsy follow-up.
required_recommendations: IV lorazepam 4 mg from the paramedics failed: give one further dose of IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg) for continuing convulsions, and no further benzodiazepine boluses once they have stopped [Glauser_2016].

Load a second-line ASM immediately, also if the convulsion has stopped, because his maintenance drug is at zero: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), his own drug, which is also one of the three agents of equivalent efficacy; IV valproate 40 mg/kg (maximum 3000 mg) is an equally acceptable choice in a man with normal liver function [ESETT_2019].

If convulsions continue after the benzodiazepine and an adequately dosed second-line agent, this is refractory status epilepticus: intubate and start an anaesthetic infusion (midazolam or propofol) under continuous EEG [Brophy_2012].
Continue video-EEG until he is back to baseline, because convulsive status can continue as non-convulsive status after the motor activity stops [Brophy_2012].

Give IV crystalloid for rhabdomyolysis (CK 1840 U/L) with repeat CK and renal function, and cool him passively for the temperature of 38.1 C; no antimicrobials and no cultures, since this is seizure-related hyperthermia.

Restart maintenance levetiracetam 1500 mg twice daily before discharge, with a dispensed supply and a refill arranged, and review whether the dose should be increased after a breakthrough episode of status epilepticus.
Counsel him on adherence, on sleep deprivation and alcohol as triggers, on what to do after a missed dose, and on local driving restrictions after a seizure; arrange epilepsy clinic follow-up.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

A temperature of 38.1 C within an hour of prolonged convulsions, with a normal temperature all day before the seizure, a procalcitonin of 0.08 ng/mL and no source, is seizure-related hyperthermia; blood cultures and an infection work-up are not indicated.

accepted: Generalized convulsive status epilepticus from levetiracetam non-adherence in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, precipitated by concurrent sleep deprivation

key_clinical_evidence: Non-adherence and sleep deprivation are the usual precipitants of breakthrough seizures in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, which needs lifelong treatment; an undetectable drug level identifies the cause and the remedy.

A convulsion that continues after one adequate benzodiazepine dose needs the second tier now: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective in ESETT, and in a generalized epilepsy the patient's own levetiracetam or valproate is preferred [ESETT_2019].
Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin, pregabalin and vigabatrin aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures in idiopathic generalized epilepsy and are avoided for maintenance.

Lactic acidosis, leukocytosis, a mildly raised troponin, a raised CK and a temperature up to 38.5 C are expected within hours of prolonged convulsions and do not by themselves indicate sepsis, infarction or infection [Brophy_2012].
Convulsive status can continue as non-convulsive status after the motor activity stops, so EEG is needed in any patient who does not return to baseline [Brophy_2012].

metadata.clinical_pearl: A convulsion that outlasts one adequate benzodiazepine dose needs the second tier at once; in a generalized epilepsy the patient's own levetiracetam or valproate is the sensible choice, and carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin and vigabatrin are avoided for maintenance because they aggravate myoclonic seizures. An undetectable drug level names both the cause and the remedy: dispense the drug and fix the refill before discharge.

patient.history_present_illness: A 36-year-old White right-handed man, a software engineer, with a 10-year history of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after a prolonged generalized convulsion at home. His girlfriend reports that at about 21:45 he had bilateral arm jerking while watching television, which within a minute evolved into a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that did not stop. She called the ambulance 5 minutes after onset and reports that he was well and afebrile all day, with no illness in the previous weeks. The paramedics gave IV lorazepam 4 mg en route without effect, and he arrived still convulsing, 22 minutes after onset. His epilepsy was confirmed by video-EEG 8 years ago, which showed generalized polyspike-wave discharges, and he has prominent myoclonic jerks on waking. He took valproate 1500 mg daily for 6 years and was switched 2 years ago to levetiracetam 1500 mg twice daily because of weight gain, with no seizures since. He ran out of levetiracetam 3 days ago, waiting for a repeat prescription, and tried to 'get by' without it. He had slept about 4 hours a night for the past week working to a deadline. He drinks a beer at weekends and had none this week, and uses no other drugs. He has no allergies. His sister has absence epilepsy.
